title: The first council
hook: elders gather at Rajagaha after the Buddha's death: Ananda recites the discourses, Upali the discipline (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
carry: held by many mouths, not just one memory

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Jataka, closed: one being, many lives. Your line: many lives, one road. Today a new part begins: what happened after the Buddha was gone.

The Buddha has died, and the monks on the road are weeping. One old monk named Subhadda tells them to stop. Don't grieve, he says. We're rid of that great ascetic who was always telling us what's proper and what isn't. Now we can do as we like. The elder Mahakassapa hears it, and he doesn't forget it. In the Vinaya, the book of monastic discipline, it is this remark that sets him to work. If the teaching isn't gathered now, he reasons, people like Subhadda will decide what it was.
screen: `THE BUDDHA HAS DIED.` → `NOW WE CAN DO AS WE LIKE.` → `KASSAPA REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Mahakassapa proposes that the elders recite the teaching and the discipline together, before anything false can take root. The Vinaya says five hundred elders were chosen to meet at Rajagaha for the rains. One almost wasn't there. Ananda had been at the Buddha's side for years and had heard him teach again and again, but he was not yet fully awakened. The text says he worked hard through the night before the council, and as he lay down to rest, before his head reached the pillow, his mind was freed. He walked into the council as one of the elders. Mahakassapa doesn't ask for speeches. He asks questions, one at a time. To Upali, a former barber who had become an expert in the monastic rules: where was the first rule laid down? About whom? In what case? Upali answers, and the discipline is recited. Then to Ananda: where was this discourse given? To whom? Ananda answers, and the discourses are recited. The Pali name for the gathering is sangiti, a chanting together. It wasn't a debate over new ideas. It was a room full of people saying the same words aloud, checking them against each other, so that the teaching would be held by many mouths and not just one memory. Some scholars ask how much of this account is history and how much is later telling. The tradition remembers it as the moment the teaching was gathered in, so it could be handed on.
screen: `RECITE IT BEFORE IT DRIFTS.` · `ANANDA, AWAKE JUST IN TIME.` · `UPALI ON RULES, ANANDA ON DISCOURSES.` · `A CHANTING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE FIRST COUNCIL.`

segments.voice: Choose something you carry by heart, a verse, a poem, a saying from someone who raised you, and say it once quietly, then again more slowly, hearing each word. Notice which words you're sure of and which ones wobble; that's how the elders checked their memory, by saying it aloud.
Sangiti. Elders gathered after the Buddha's death to recite his teaching and his rules aloud, together. Today's word.
Your line: held by many mouths, not just one memory. It all grew from one careless remark. Day eight hundred fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: Theravada monks still recite texts together in chanting sessions, and the tradition looks back to this first council as the moment its teachings were gathered and fixed.

chat.says: What actually happened at the first Buddhist council?
options: Elders recited the teaching and rules aloud together, question by question.
Leaders debated and voted in new teachings the Buddha never gave.
Ananda wrote the Buddha's words down in a book for the first time.
chat.meaning: It was a sangiti, a chanting together: Upali answered on the discipline, Ananda on the discourses, so many mouths held the teaching.

Mahakassapa.meaning: the elder who called the first council

Rajagaha.meaning: the city where the first council met

Upali.meaning: the former barber who recited the rules

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga 11 (the council of the five hundred)

notes: All texts paraphrased; nothing quoted. Subhadda's remark is paraphrased from Cullavagga 11.1.1 (also in Digha Nikaya 16).
'Five hundred' is stated because Cullavagga 11 gives it; the text says five hundred less one were chosen before Ananda was added. Simplified; confirm.
Ananda described only as having heard the Buddha teach 'again and again' (no superlative); tradition calls him foremost among the learned. 'For years' left vague on purpose (no number).
Upali 'a former barber': from the Vinaya account of the Sakyan princes' going forth (Cullavagga 7); confirm.
Location detail (Sattapanni cave) left out because it comes from later commentary, not Cullavagga 11.
'Some scholars ask how much of this account is history': attributed to some scholars only; confirm wording.
First day of Block E (After the Buddha).
Editor pass: 'the master of the monastic rules' softened to 'an expert in' (no superlative the cited chapter gives).
Audit: 'not a debate or a vote' softened, since Cullavagga 11 does record formal motions (the minor rules, Ananda's faults).
